target_customer: Consumers and workers who make presentations in the browser, plus developers using the Cappuccino framework
problem: Presentation software required desktop installs; 280 Slides offered a Keynote like editor in the browser with PowerPoint import and export.
business_model: Free web application and open source framework; no revenue model found
product_category: Web based presentation app and web application framework

competitors.name: SlideRocket
competitors.what: Online presentation app built in Flash

technical_complexity.rationale: Built a Cocoa style framework (Cappuccino) with its own Objective-J language to run a desktop quality editor in the browser in 2008.

defensibility.rationale: The framework was open source and presentations were a crowded category; the engineering talent was the main asset.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Google Docs offered presentations; Motorola bought the team and Cappuccino in summer 2010 to strengthen its Android app work.

market_need_then: Online office apps were growing in 2008 with Google Docs and Zoho, and developers wanted desktop quality web apps; reviewers found 280 Slides elegant though less full featured than PowerPoint.

branding.community_and_virality: Cappuccino framework drew open source developers; the Slashdot and HN discussions covered the launch

brand_strength.rationale: Known to developers through Cappuccino and to early adopters through 280 Slides; no evidence of mass brand recognition.

outcome_analysis: 280 North launched 280 Slides in June 2008 and built the Cappuccino framework, raising only about 250,000 in angel money. Motorola acquired it in summer 2010 for a reported 20 million to gain web app engineering talent; Motorola declined to disclose terms and later kept the Atlas tool private. It reads as a capital efficient technical team acquisition.
notes: The 20M price is an unconfirmed report; Motorola stated terms were not disclosed. No company website listed in the directory.
